transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-14
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Asha Rao (Luminex Head of ML), Tom Diaz (Infra Lead), Priya Nair (PM)

Summary (auto):
Quick console walkthrough focused on per-path usage analytics, cost decomposition by route, and options for pilot — hosted vs dedicated vs private. Customer concerned about latency for clinical inference, cost attribution to product teams, and SOC2/KMS alignment. Redwood team to send pricing & benchmark assets and draft pilot scope.

Topics:
- Path-level dashboards and filters
- Token-level cost attribution and SLOs
- Batching/KV cache impact on unit economics
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
- Security: SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs, data residency
- Next steps: pilot proposal and benchmark scripts

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we are a little early but we'll get started. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE for the healthcare vertical. Jordan our SE is here also, he'll run the console sections.
[00:15] Asha: Hi Maya, hi Jordan. We're excited — Luminex has a few questions about how we'd be able to attribute costs per product path, like triage vs summarize vs clinical decision support.
[00:25] Maya: Totally. Today's brief is mostly console-first, show you the path economics views, then we'll jump into the model + routing recommendations. Jordan?
[00:32] Jordan: Yep. I'll share my screen. Just a note, some of the labels in our export can come through as "routes" or "paths" depending on how you instrument requests, so I'll show both views.
[00:45] [00:45] Jordan: Ok, top-level is the usage dashboard. You can see token volume, latency distribution, and cost over time. Over here is the path filter — you can drill into a specific API route, or group by product team.
[01:05] Tom: Can that map to our internal service names? We have 20-ish endpoints and we'd like each to be charged to a team.
[01:12] Jordan: Yes, you can either instrument a header like x-redwood-route or we can map at ingestion using your telemetry ID. We also support mapping rules in the console to translate route names.
[01:27] [01:27] Jordan: Here's an example from a customer where we show 1) tokens per route 2) cost per route 3) effective cost per 1k responses. The UI lets you toggle model variant (quantized vs fp16) and see the cost delta.
[01:42] Priya: I saw something about kv-cache earlier in the doc we read. How much does a cache help per-path? Our triage flow is very repetitive.
[01:50] Jordan: Great question. KV-cache (sometimes transcribed as KV-cash, sorry the transcript does that) reduces repeated prefix compute. For a high reuse flow like triage, we've seen 40-60% token cost reduction because the prefix tokens are hot. You can see the cache hit rate visualization here.
[02:10] Asha: And that hits across hosted and dedicated?
[02:15] Jordan: Yes, caching is in the runtime. On hosted it's automatic per-tenant; on Dedicated you get pinned pools and more control over cache sizing per pool. For Private deployments, you can enable local cache but you manage persistence settings.
[02:30] [02:30] Tom: Latency is the big constraint — clinical inference must be under 200ms p95. Can Redwood meet that while keeping costs reasonable?
[02:40] Maya: There's a tradeoff. For 200ms p95 you typically go hosted with the lowest latency model variant or a dedicated pinned GPU pool — dedicated gives you consistent latency but at higher reserved cost. Jordan will show an example SLO policy.
[02:55] [02:55] Jordan: Right, on this per-route dashboard you can set SLOs per route and we show estimated cost to maintain that SLO based on traffic patterns. For example, route A (triage) needs 200ms and has bursty traffic; the model choice plus autoscale policy changes the cost curve here.
[03:20] Priya: There's a lot of numbers. Can we export a monthly chargeback report for Finance?
[03:26] Jordan: Absolutely. There's an export button that snapshots per-path spend for the selected window. We can also push to your billing system via S3 drop or webhooks.
[03:40] [03:40] Asha: Regulatory question — we need SOC 2 type 2 and need keys in our HSM. Does Redwood support customer-managed KMS/HSM?
[03:51] Maya: Yes, for Private deployments we support KMS integration and HSMs. For Dedicated there's an option to integrate with your cloud KMS for encryption-at-rest and in-transit is TLS with mutual auth. We have SOC2 and ISO attestations; I'll attach the security pack.
[04:10] Tom: Audit logs? We need request-level audit trails for a year.
[04:15] Jordan: We persist request metadata and provide audit exports. Retention policies are configurable; there's an add-on for longer retention and we've done year-plus for enterprise customers.
[04:28] [04:28] Maya: Quick aside — some customers confuse "Redwood Private" vs "Redwood Dedica" — Dedica meaning Dedicated — sorry for the shorthand — we can outline the pricing differences in the followup.
[04:40] Asha: No worries. Could you show a concrete route example?
[04:44] Jordan: Sure. I'm opening route: /clinical/summarize. You can see tokens in/out, model used, cost breakdown: compute, caching savings, and rounding. If we switch model from 'rw-base-8q' to 'rw-compact-16' you see cost up/down and slight latency change.
[05:05] [05:05] Jordan: Note the "effective tokens" column — we normalize generation tokens and prompt tokens for cost math. We also estimate price impact for batching; enable the batching slider to simulate larger batch sizes and see how it reduces per-token cost but increases queuing latency.
[05:25] Priya: For our decision support path the hallucination tolerance is low; we prefer bigger models. How do we balance that with cost?
[05:33] Jordan: Two levers: route-level model pins + quality monitoring. We can pin the path to a higher-quality model and run sampling-based regressions — Redwood Optimize suggests quantization profiles or caching to bring cost down without quality regressions.
[05:50] Asha: Can Optimize recommend configurations automatically?
[05:55] Jordan: Yes, Optimize will run offline suggestions based on your telemetry — it suggests batching thresholds, quantization, and model variants per route, along with an estimated cost delta and probable quality impact.
[06:10] [06:10] Maya: Let me show the routing policy panel — you can set fallback chains. So route X tries low-cost variant first, if quality check fails or latency spikes it can fallback to a pinned higher tier. That keeps availability up and controls spend.
[06:30] Tom: Fallbacks sound useful. Does that work cross-region? We have data residency rules in EU and US.
[06:36] Jordan: Smart routing supports region policies. You can define that EU traffic stays in EU and fallback to another EU region or to on-prem if you have Redwood Private in your region.
[06:50] Priya: On the console screenshots I noticed a "route health" score — what's that based on?
[06:56] Jordan: It's a composite: error rate, latency violations, cost variance, and quality regression signals from your eval sets. We weight them; you can customize thresholds per route.
[07:12] [07:12] Asha: For pilot we're thinking 3 routes: triage, summarize, and decision-support. We want to measure cost per 1k responses and p95 latency impact. How would you recommend we start?
[07:24] Maya: Typical pilot is 4-6 weeks: week 1 onboarding + telemetry mapping, week 2 baseline benchmarks on your traffic, week 3 run Optimize suggestions and KV-cache tuning, week 4 production pilot with canary routing. Jordan will ship scripts to reproduce your baseline.
[07:40] Jordan: I'll share a benchmark checklist — it's lightweight: sample payloads, average and p95 sizes, expected concurrency, auth header mapping. Also a small KV-cache test harness.
[07:55] Tom: What about bursting? Some of our endpoints have unpredictable spikes tied to event windows.
[08:02] Jordan: We support burst capacity on Dedicated and hosted tiers. For Dedicated you can have a burst bucket that spins up extra nodes; for hosted we do dynamic autoscale and can escalate to higher-cost compute when needed. The console shows estimated burst costs under different traffic shapes.
[08:20] [08:20] Priya: Any pitfalls others have run into when mapping paths to teams?
[08:25] Jordan: Two things: 1) naming conventions matter — try to instrument consistent route identifiers. 2) watch for shared utils that call downstream models — these can double-count tokens if not instrumented properly. We show an example mapping rule to dedupe cross-calls.
[08:40] Maya: Also, suggest a short-lived internal alignment session between infra and product so we map routes correctly — prevents finance surprises.
[08:50] Asha: Makes sense. Could you show the billing snapshot export?
[08:53] Jordan: Exporting now. The CSV has columns: route, team, tokens, cost_compute, cost_net, cache_savings, model_variant. You can also schedule monthly exports.
[09:10] [09:10] Priya: How granular is cost visibility? Can we see per-request cost?
[09:15] Jordan: We avoid per-request price display in the UI for performance, but the export can include per-request token counts if you need it for detailed chargebacks. That's typically used for audit or dispute resolution.
[09:30] Tom: Security again — SSO/SAML and RBAC? We want team-level permissions so Product can't change infra settings.
[09:37] Maya: RBAC is supported, role templates for product, infra, finance. SAML SSO integrates with IdPs; for Private we can do LDAP mapping as well.
[09:50] [09:50] Asha: Any examples where customers reduced costs 30%+ using Optimize and caching?
[09:56] Jordan: Yes, one health customer with a lot of repetitive triage saw 55% token cost drop after enabling KV-cache and adjusting batching. They also used a mixed model routing to keep decision-support on a large model while moving summarization to a quantized variant.
[10:15] Priya: For the pilot, do we need a contract or can we do a short eval on hosted?
[10:20] Maya: We can run a pilot on hosted with a short-term seat and usage caps. If you prefer guaranteed performance we recommend Dedicated pilot. Both are common; we'll include options in the follow-up.
[10:35] [10:35] Jordan: Quick demo of the quality monitoring: you can upload a set of prompts and expected outputs. The console runs periodic checks and flags regressions. That ties into alerts for route health.
[10:52] Asha: How do you handle model rollouts? We don't want regressions after a model update.
[10:57] Jordan: Rollouts are canary by default — you can do percentage-based rollouts and automatic rollback on quality regressions. We keep model version history and diff metrics.
[11:12] Priya: Can we run local on-premise inference for sensitive PHI?
[11:18] Maya: Yes, Redwood Private supports on-prem packaging. For PHI we usually recommend Private with your KMS/HSM and strict network controls. There is an ops package and a support plan for air-gapped installs.
[11:35] [11:35] Tom: A couple nitty gritty questions: what metrics do you use to estimate cost in the SLO calculator?
[11:40] Jordan: We use observed token length distributions, concurrency, model throughput on chosen instance types, KV-cache hit rates, and batching assumptions. The estimator gives a probabilistic cost range.
[11:55] Asha: Any limitations on instrumentation? We use envoy sidecars and have a custom header pipeline.
[12:02] Jordan: Envoy is fine. The easiest approach is to forward a route header from your sidecar; we also have collectors that ingest OpenTelemetry spans. If you want we can run a short mapping script.
[12:15] [12:15] Maya: Quick check — is procurement on the call or do you want legal involved later?
[12:19] Priya: Legal will get involved before production but not for pilot. Procurement will want estimated monthly cost.
[12:25] Maya: We'll provide a sample pilot SOW and estimated run cost.
[12:30] [12:30] Jordan: I'm going to show billing anomaly detection — it looks for spikes in tokens per route and surface suspects. Useful for catching runaway loops in code that call the API repeatedly.
[12:48] Tom: Nice. Do you have rate limits per route?
[12:52] Jordan: Yes, per-route throttles and global quotas are available. We can set soft and hard limits.
[13:02] Priya: If we proceed, timeline — how quickly can we get pilot telemetry mapped?
[13:07] Jordan: Typically 3-7 business days to map telemetry and get baseline results assuming you can share sample traffic and a test key.
[13:20] Asha: Ok that works. Any tricky bits with our compliance systems? We use a custom key rotation cadence.
[13:26] Maya: We can accommodate custom rotation via KMS integrations for Private; for hosted we'll sync on rotation windows and provide key-handling docs.
[13:40] [13:40] Jordan: Wrapping up the console tour — again the key artifacts: per-path spend, exportable chargeback CSVs, health scores, Optimize recommendations, and routing policies.
[13:55] Maya: Next steps recap — we'll send: 1) tailored pricing + sample path export, 2) benchmark checklist + KV-cache script, 3) pilot SOW draft. Any additions?
[14:06] Asha: Please include estimated cost to maintain 200ms p95 for triage route.
[14:11] Maya: Noted. Jordan anything else?
[14:14] Jordan: I'll include a short how-to for instrumenting headers from Envoy and a mapping example.
[14:20] Priya: Great. Thanks, everyone.
[14:22] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up by end of week.
[14:25] Asha: Thanks.
